title: Multiple myeloma bone disease: tumor-driven osteoclast activation
vignette: A 66-year-old man comes to the office due to several weeks of back and lower extremity pain. The pain feels dull and achy and is worsened by movement, causing him to have difficulty bearing weight and ambulating. He has had no bladder or bowel dysfunction, extremity weakness, or numbness. The patient takes metformin for type 2 diabetes mellitus. He drinks 2 alcoholic beverages daily. Physical examination shows no gross abnormality or deformity of the back or extremities. There is no swelling or redness of the legs, and neurological examination is normal. A radiograph of the right lower extremity shows a well-defined, purely radiolucent (osteolytic) lesion without surrounding sclerosis. Laboratory results show hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5), creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, calcium 11.0 mg/dL (normal 8.4-10.2), total protein 8.8 g/dL (normal 6.0-7.8), and albumin 3.8 g/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's bone changes?

clues.text: purely radiolucent (osteolytic) lesion without surrounding sclerosis
clues.note: A purely lytic (radiolucent) bone lesion with NO sclerotic rim is characteristic of multiple myeloma - myeloma uniquely activates osteoclasts AND inhibits osteoblasts, so there's no bone-forming (blastic) response.
Normocytic anemia (Hb 9.6 / normal 13.5-17.5) from marrow infiltration by plasma cells - part of the myeloma 'CRAB' picture.
Hypercalcemia (Ca 11.0 / normal 8.4-10.2) from osteolysis - the 'C' of CRAB (hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions).

An elevated total protein (8.8 / normal 6.0-7.8) with a relatively normal albumin implies excess GLOBULIN - a monoclonal paraprotein (M-spike) from the plasma cell clone. Anemia + hypercalcemia + high protein + renal insufficiency = multiple myeloma.

whatMatters: Older man with bone pain, a purely lytic lesion, normocytic anemia, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, and an elevated total protein (paraprotein gap) = multiple myeloma (CRAB). Myeloma cells secrete factors (RANK-L, and osteoblast inhibitors) that cause LOCAL TUMOR-MEDIATED ACTIVATION OF OSTEOCLASTS (with osteoblast inhibition), producing purely osteolytic lesions. Answer E.
strategy: Assemble CRAB (hyperCalcemia, Renal, Anemia, Bone lesions) + high total protein -> multiple myeloma. Then explain the bone changes: myeloma stimulates osteoCLASTS (via RANK-L) and inhibits osteoBLASTS -> purely lytic lesions. Answer E. Reject: PTH/vitamin D excess (would raise those hormones and not give an M-spike/anemia), decreased urinary calcium (thiazide - increases density), and osteoBLAST activation (would make sclerotic, not lytic, lesions).

options.text: Local tumor cell-mediated activation of osteoblasts
Local tumor cell-mediated activation of osteoclasts

eliminations.label: Decreased urinary calcium excretion - thiazide-like
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: reduced renal calcium excretion (e.g., thiazide diuretics) can raise serum calcium. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it INCREASES bone density and wouldn't produce lytic lesions, anemia, or a paraprotein. ✅ Correct if: thiazide-associated mild hypercalcemia.

eliminations.label: Increased 1,25-vitamin D - granulomatous
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: excess active vitamin D (e.g., sarcoidosis) raises calcium by boosting gut absorption. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it doesn't cause purely lytic lesions with anemia and an M-spike. ✅ Correct if: granulomatous disease with hypercalcemia.

eliminations.label: Increased PTH - hyperparathyroidism, your pick
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: primary hyperparathyroidism raises calcium via PTH-driven bone resorption. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: PTH excess causes different bone changes (osteitis fibrosa cystica/subperiosteal resorption) and does NOT explain the anemia, elevated total protein, or renal failure of myeloma. ✅ Correct if: primary hyperparathyroidism (high PTH, high calcium, low phosphate).

eliminations.label: OsteoBLAST activation - would be sclerotic
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: tumor activation of osteoblasts causes bone FORMATION (osteoblastic/sclerotic lesions, e.g., prostate cancer mets). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: myeloma INHIBITS osteoblasts, giving purely lytic (radiolucent) lesions - the opposite of blastic. ✅ Correct if: osteoblastic metastases (prostate cancer).

reasoning: Purely lytic bone lesion + normocytic anemia + hypercalcemia + renal insufficiency + high total protein = multiple myeloma (CRAB)
Myeloma plasma cells secrete RANK-L and osteoblast inhibitors
-> local activation of osteoCLASTS and inhibition of osteoBLASTS
mechanism: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy that produces monoclonal immunoglobulin (paraprotein) and classically causes the CRAB features: hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia (normocytic), and Bone lesions. Malignant plasma cells proliferate in the marrow and secrete cytokines that stimulate osteoCLAST maturation and activity (via RANK-ligand) while simultaneously secreting factors that INHIBIT osteoblasts (e.g., IL-3, IL-7, Wnt pathway inhibitors). This uncoupling tips bone remodeling strongly toward resorption, producing LOCAL TUMOR-MEDIATED OSTEOCLAST ACTIVATION with purely radiolucent (osteolytic) lesions and no reactive sclerosis, along with hypercalcemia (from osteolysis) and bone pain. Because osteoblasts are suppressed, myeloma is one of the few tumors to cause purely lytic lesions (most others show some osteoblastic/sclerotic reaction). The distractors (decreased urinary calcium, excess 1,25-vitamin D, excess PTH, osteoblast activation) either raise bone density or fail to explain the anemia, paraprotein, and lytic lesions.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Heme/Onc > multiple myeloma: monoclonal plasma cells, CRAB, purely lytic lesions from osteoclast activation (RANK-L) + osteoblast inhibition; Rouleaux, M-spike, Bence Jones protein.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Assemble CRAB + elevated total protein into myeloma, then explain the LYTIC lesions by osteoclast activation (not osteoblast).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on osteolytic/radiolucent, osteoclast vs osteoblast, RANK-L, paraprotein/M-spike, or CRAB? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Increased PTH (your pick) doesn't explain the anemia/paraprotein/renal failure; osteoBLAST activation would make sclerotic (not lytic) lesions.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.message: The radiograph shows a purely radiolucent 'punched-out' lytic lesion without a sclerotic rim - the myeloma signature (osteoclast-driven, osteoblast-suppressed). Anchor: 'punched-out lytic = myeloma.'

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: CRAB + high total protein + purely lytic lesions = multiple myeloma; osteoclast activation (RANK-L) + osteoblast inhibition.
